Caveat, not an error: p. 16 says each writer produced four metaphors, but Tab. S1 holds 2,493 metaphor observations for 644 writers, 83 fewer than 2,576. The loss is in outputs, not writers, because N writer stays 644. The paper does not explain it. If the 65 terminated sessions are outside the 644, at least 709 people began the task and about 9 percent did not reach the analysis. The paper does not say which reading is true.

confirmed.statement: No text, table, or figure prints writers by arm, so the null arm counts are right. Figs. 1-4 and S1-S9 show no n, and Fig. S10 gives only n = 2,235 metaphors. The p. 8 shares (84 of 228 L2 writers chose their native language: 39 percent in AI ideation, 34 percent in AI refinement) fit 26 integer splits, from 109 to 148 L2 writers in AI ideation, so they fix no arm count.

Caveat, not an error: Tab. S3 prints N writer = 441 in the AI-arm rating model and 440 in the AI-arm diversity model. Both full models hold the same 644 writers, so the two AI-arm counts should agree, and the paper does not explain the one-writer gap. The form records both values. Its note that the human-only arm holds 203 writers (644 - 441) is stated as conditional. The 440 column gives 204 (106 L1). Both readings put 98 L2 writers (326 - 228) in human-only.

Caveat, not an error, outside the people fields: 351 evaluators who rated 24 metaphors each give 8,424 ratings, but the rating models hold 8,241, which is 183 fewer. The AI-arm model holds 5,638 ratings, above the 5,616 (351 x 16) that drawing 'in equal numbers from the three writing conditions' allows. The split follows the metaphor counts instead, at about 3.3 ratings per metaphor in each arm. The paper explains neither gap. These are ratings, so no people count changes. The S1-O6 measure_detail repeats the p. 16 equal-draw design without this conflict.

confirmed.statement: The 'who', 'population', and 'country' fields match p. 16. L1 writers had English as their sole native language and were born and residing in a majority-English-speaking country. L2 writers named 34 native languages, led by Arabic (15 percent), Portuguese (13), Italian (11), Polish (10), and Spanish (9). Writers averaged 36.1 years (SD 12.6, range 18-79), were 49 percent women and 66 percent White, were recruited on Prolific, and received 3.5 pounds for a median 20 minutes. The participants quote is verbatim.

Inside the paper, S2 reuses the S1 writers. The authors built a persona from every writer's background questionnaire and compared the simulated pools with the S1 human pools. S2 recruits no one, so its null counts and counts_are 'other' are right, and no person is counted twice.

summary: The PDF supports every people count in the c054 form: S1 analyzes 644 writers (p. 16, and N writer = 644 in Tab. S1, p. 28, and Tab. S2, p. 29), the paper prints no count at allocation or by arm, the 65 tab-switch terminations (24, 23, 18) are recorded as sessions, and S2 recruits no one. Three caveats leave the coding unchanged (83 metaphors and 183 ratings missing without explanation, and AI-arm writer counts of 441 and 440 in Tab. S3), so criterion 2 holds on S1 alone, while random assignment (criterion 1) is a separate question that this check does not settle.
